lead: Isaiah sings of a desert that blooms, of the blind and the lame healed, and of a holy road home. In Luke the song reaches a crowded house: friends open a roof, and Jesus, seeing their faith, forgives a paralysed man and then tells him to walk. Isaiah says, “He will come and save you”; the Gospel shows him doing it, and shows that the deepest wound he heals is sin.

set: This chapter follows a dark vision of judgment on Edom (Isaiah 34), and its language is so close to chapters 40–55 that many scholars see it as closely related to them. It speaks of a road home through a desert transformed. Yesterday we heard the call to build the road (40:3). Today we see who walks on it.
str: vv. 1–2: the desert rejoices and blossoms.
vv. 3–4: strengthen the weak: “Here is your God.”
vv. 5–7: the blind, deaf, lame and mute healed; water in the desert.
vv. 8–10: the Holy Way; the ransomed return to Zion with singing.
kw: A spring flower of the dry lands. The exact plant is uncertain. It appears here and in the Song of Songs (2:1). The point is a colour no one expected in the waste.
No ordinary road: God has set it apart. It recalls the pilgrim roads to Zion, and it also becomes a name for life with God. The first Christians were called people of “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
The gō’ēl was the relative who paid to buy back a family member from debt or slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49). God acts here as the next of kin of his people.
vv: Say to those who are of a fearful heart, “Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God. He will come with vengeance, with terrible recompense. He will come and save you.”
“Vengeance” here means that God will set right what was done to his people. Its last word is “save”.
Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped
These are the very signs Jesus names for the disciples of John: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, … the deaf hear” (Matthew 11:5). Today's Gospel gives one of them.
And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
Sorrow and sighing are pictured as intruders who run away when the procession arrives. Everything sad has at last been made to leave.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' healings are messianic signs, which announce a far greater liberation: from the slavery of sin (CCC 549). The Church reads Isaiah 35 in Advent so that we may recognise him when he comes. The Holy Way is now open in Christ, who says, “I am the way” (John 14:6).

set: This is the first time Pharisees appear in Luke, together with teachers of the law from Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem. They are serious, observant men, who have come to find out about a new teacher. The scene opens a series of five disputes (5:17–6:11). Luke is careful to note at the start: “the power of the Lord was with him to heal.”
str: v. 17: the audience and the power.
vv. 18–19: the friends and the roof.
vv. 21–24: the question and the answer.
vv. 25–26: the man walks; everyone glorifies God.
kw: Literally “man” or “O human being”, as the Malayalam POC keeps it. It is a plain and direct form of address.
Power that is rightfully held. Daniel 7:13–14 shows one like a Son of Man receiving authority from God. Jesus claims it “on earth”, here and now.
Literally things beyond expectation. We have the word “paradox” from it. “We have seen strange things today”: sēmeron, today, is a key word of Luke's Gospel (2:11; 4:21; 19:9; 23:43).
vv: When he saw their faith, he said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven you.”

“Their” faith: Jesus looks at the friends, and the man is healed because of what they did. This is the root of all intercession. Jesus does not say that the man's sickness was his punishment; he goes first to the deepest need.
Who is this who is speaking blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?
The question is correct, and their theology is sound: only God forgives sins. The only thing they have not yet seen is who is standing in front of them.
Immediately he stood up before them, took what he had been lying on, and went to his home, glorifying God.
The visible sign supports the invisible gift. The bed that carried him he now carries. He leaves by the door, and he and the crowd end up doing the same thing: glorifying God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that “only God forgives sins”, and that Jesus, as Son of God, exercises this divine power and gives it to men in his name (CCC 1441). It opens its teaching on the sacraments of healing with this very scene: Christ, physician of soul and body, who forgave the paralytic and restored him, willed that his Church continue this work (CCC 1421). St Ambrose, whose memorial is today, comments on this passage in his book on Luke: how great is the Lord, who forgives some for the merit of others (in substance).

qa: Did the man's paralysis come from his sins?

The text does not say so. Some in that time took sickness to be a punishment for sin, but Jesus rejects this as a general rule (John 9:2–3). He treats both needs because he is the healer of the whole person (CCC 1503). Sin, not paralysis, is the deeper bondage, and that is why it comes first.
rite: St Ambrose (died 397), governor at Milan and still a catechumen, was acclaimed bishop by the people, and was ordained on 7 December 374, the date of today's memorial. He preached so well that he helped bring St Augustine to the faith, and he baptised him at Easter in 387. He is one of the great Doctors of the Latin Church. He wrote the Advent hymn Veni, Redemptor gentium, and he spoke of Mary as a type of the Church (Lumen Gentium 63). His memorial stands just before tomorrow's Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception, and in a sense he prepares us to keep it: to look at Mary is to see what the Church is called to be.
study: Who has carried me to Jesus when I could not go myself? Whom could I carry by my prayer and my faith today?
When did I last hear the words “your sins are forgiven”? What keeps me from going to confession this Advent?
